Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette: Clara Vance was sixty-two when the river breached the levee. She remembered the suddenness of it-the way the water did not creep but surged, filling her ground-floor studio, where she worked as a graphic designer, in under ten minutes. Her drafting tables were swallowed first, followed by the heavy rolls of paper that had defined her career. When she finally waded through the chest-deep current to the stairs, the door to her workspace had been wrenched off its hinges by the force of the water, slamming against the wall with a crack that echoed in the empty house. In the days that followed, while neighbors gathered in a gymnasium waiting for relief buses, the air grew thick with the smell of alcohol from supply tents where exhausted volunteers poured drinks to steady their hands. When a relief coordinator gathered the displaced to announce another missing person, Clara had to turn away; the mere talk of people losing loved ones sent her pulse spiking, and she began avoiding community halls altogether. She told herself she could not be there, though she had come to believe her beliefs about how the world worked had been completely destroyed, replaced by something unpredictable and cruel. She was certain that what happened to her was deeply unfair, that the authorities had looked the other way, and nothing had been done. Over the following months, Clara's days fell into a rigid rhythm. She found herself circling the same questions: if she had raised the generators earlier, if she had moved the client files to the second floor, if she had heeded the county warnings sooner. The thoughts would loop until her chest tightened. In the kitchen, she found herself wiping her counters repeatedly, aligning the knives, reloading the dishwasher, and taking them out again until every surface gleamed. She returned to this routine again and again, seeking a sense of control she could not find elsewhere. When the memories of the flood surfaced, they rarely arrived as coherent stories. Sometimes she could recall what happened but felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. Other times, the water seemed to rise in her own hallway, the damp concrete pressing against her throat, making her certain she was standing in it again. On those days, the event felt so extreme, so impossibly severe, that she was certain it could not have actually happened to her. She would press her palms flat against the wall, telling herself she had to erase the memory of the event entirely, though the images persisted. Her home studio became a site of tension. When the heavy oak door to her workspace opened too quickly, the sharp report of the latch would freeze her mid-step. She stopped entering the room after the third time she had dropped a client's layout proofs on the floor, startled by the sound. Instead, she began leaving her laptop in the living room, reorganizing her digital archives by color and date until her fingers ached. Her husband noticed the quiet withdrawal first. He stopped asking about her work schedules, and she stopped explaining why she could not meet her usual deadlines. The months blurred into a steady pattern of vigilance and retreat. Now, at seventy-eight, Clara sat across from a clinician for the first time, her hands folded tightly in her lap. She had come because the silence between the door clicks and the smell of rain on pavement had become too loud to bear, and because she was tired of waking up certain she was standing in rising water. What she hoped for was simply to walk into her studio without bracing for the slam, and to trust that she might still be able to navigate the days ahead.
